lessons.title: Primary Treatment: Sedimentation, Filtration, and Coagulation
lessons.body:
Primary treatment removes the bulk of dirt, sand, and organic matter from your raw water before it hits expensive filters. Start with sedimentation: pump raw water into a settling tank or large drum and let it sit for 2â4 hours. Heavy particles sink. In many African settings, you can use a simple 1000-litre tank with a drain valve at the bottom to flush out the sludge. If your water is cloudy (turbidity above 10 NTU), add coagulation chemicals. Aluminium sulphate (alum) is cheap and widely available. Dose 10â30 mg per litre of waterâroughly 10â30 grams per 1000 litres. Dissolve the alum in a small bucket of clean water first, then stir it into the tank for 2 minutes, then stir slowly for 15 minutes. This makes tiny particles clump into flocs that settle faster. After 1â2 hours of settling, drain the clear water from the top into a filtration unit.

Filtration comes next. A rapid sand filter is a tank with layers of gravel (bottom), coarse sand, and fine sand (top). Water flows down through the sand, trapping remaining particles. You must backwash the filter every 1â2 days by pushing clean water upward to flush out trapped dirt. For small-scale bottling (500â2000 litres per day), a simple pressure sand filter with a 50-micron cartridge after it works well. Replace cartridges when pressure drops by 0.5 bar.

If you cannot afford alum, use moringa seeds: crush 1â2 seeds per litre, mix with water, and add to the tank. The natural proteins act as a coagulant. This is common in rural Kenya and Nigeria. Always test your treated water with a turbidity meter (or a simple Secchi disk) to ensure it is below 5 NTU before moving to fine filtration. Never skip sedimentationâit saves money on filters and chemicals downstream.

lessons.title: Reverse Osmosis and Nanofiltration Systems
lessons.body:
Reverse osmosis (RO) forces water through a semi-permeable membrane that rejects 95â99% of dissolved salts, heavy metals, and bacteria. For bottled water, RO is the workhorse for treating brackish or high-TDS water. A typical small RO system for 500 litres per hour uses a 4-inch membrane, a high-pressure pump (10â15 bar), and pre-filters (5-micron sediment and carbon block). You must pretreat water with antiscalant (2â5 mg/L) to prevent scaling, especially if your water is hard. In Africa, many boreholes have TDS above 1000 mg/L; RO brings it down to 50â150 mg/L, which is ideal for drinking water.

Nanofiltration (NF) is similar but uses a looser membrane. It rejects 50â90% of salts, including most hardness (calcium and magnesium) but lets some beneficial minerals through. NF operates at lower pressure (5â10 bar) and wastes less water (10â20% reject vs. 30â50% for RO). If your source water has moderate TDS (300â800 mg/L) and you want to keep some taste, NF is a good choice. However, RO is more common because it guarantees consistent low TDS, which helps with blending later.

Key maintenance: replace pre-filters every 1â3 months, clean membranes every 3â6 months with a caustic/acid wash, and replace membranes every 2â3 years. Always install a flow meter and pressure gauges. A sudden drop in permeate flow means fouling. In many African countries, power fluctuations can damage pumpsâuse a voltage stabiliser. Also, the reject water (concentrate) can be reused for cleaning floors or irrigation, but not for drinking. Test your product water with a TDS meter daily; aim for 10â50 mg/L for RO permeate. If TDS is higher, check membrane integrity.

lessons.title: Distillation and Deionization Processes
lessons.body:
Distillation removes nearly all impurities by boiling water into steam and condensing it back to liquid. It kills microbes and leaves behind salts, heavy metals, and most organics. For small-scale bottling, a simple solar still or electric distiller can produce 5â20 litres per day. But distillation is energy-intensive: boiling 1 litre of water takes about 0.7 kWh of electricity. In Africa, where grid power may be unreliable or expensive, distillation is usually reserved for high-value products (e.g., laboratory water or specialty bottled water). If you use a solar still, you need 2â3 square metres of glass or plastic cover per litre per day. The condensate is very pure (TDS < 5 mg/L) but flat-tasting and slightly acidic (pH 6.5â7.0). You must remineralise it before bottling.

Deionization (DI) uses ion-exchange resins to remove dissolved ions. Water passes through a cation resin (releases H+ ions) and an anion resin (releases OH- ions), producing ultra-pure water with TDS < 1 mg/L. DI is not a disinfectantâit does not kill bacteriaâso you must pre-treat with UV or ozone. DI resins need regeneration with hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide, which is dangerous and requires proper training. For most African bottling startups, DI is overkill. Instead, use RO followed by a mixed-bed DI cartridge if you need very low TDS for a specific product (e.g., water for baby formula).

A practical alternative: if your water is already low in TDS (< 200 mg/L), you can skip distillation and DI entirely. Use RO only when TDS is high. For distilled or DI water, add a mineral blend (see Lesson 6) to bring TDS to 50â150 mg/L and pH to 7.0â7.5. Always test with a conductivity meter. Store distilled water in stainless steel or glassânot plasticâbecause pure water can leach chemicals from some plastics.

lessons.title: Ozonation and UV Light Disinfection
lessons.body:
Disinfection is the final barrier against bacteria, viruses, and parasites. Ozone (O3) is a powerful gas that kills microbes 3,000 times faster than chlorine. In bottled water plants, ozone is generated on-site from air or oxygen and injected into water via a venturi or bubble diffuser. Dose 0.2â0.5 mg/L for 4â10 minutes contact time. Ozone also removes colour, taste, and odour. After treatment, ozone decays to oxygen within 20â30 minutes, leaving no chemical residue. However, ozone is toxic to breatheâinstall an ozone destruct unit and ventilate the room. In Africa, small ozone generators (5â10 g/h) cost $200â$500 and run on 220V. They are common in Kenya, Nigeria, and South Africa. Test residual ozone with a DPD kit; aim for 0.1â0.2 mg/L after 10 minutes.

UV light (254 nm) is a physical disinfectant. Water flows past a UV lamp inside a quartz sleeve. The UV dose must be at least 40 mJ/cm2 to inactivate bacteria and viruses. For a flow rate of 500 L/h, you need a 25â30 W UV lamp. Change the lamp every 9,000 hours (about 12 months). Clean the quartz sleeve weekly with a soft cloth and vinegar to remove scaleâscale blocks UV light. UV does not leave residual, so it is best used after ozone or with a small chlorine dose (0.2â0.5 mg/L) to protect against recontamination in bottles. In many African cities, UV units are sold as âwater purifiersâ for homes; for bottling, buy a commercial stainless-steel UV reactor with a UV intensity monitor. Always pre-filter water to < 5 microns before UVâparticles can shield microbes. Combine ozone and UV for a robust, chemical-free disinfection train.

lessons.title: Activated Carbon Filtration for Taste and Odor Removal
lessons.body:
Activated carbon (AC) removes chlorine, pesticides, industrial solvents, and the earthy-musty compounds (geosmin and 2-MIB) that make water taste bad. It works by adsorption: contaminants stick to the carbonâs huge internal surface area (one gram has 500â1500 m2). For bottled water, use granular activated carbon (GAC) in a pressure vessel or carbon block cartridges. A typical GAC filter for 1000 L/h has a bed depth of 60â90 cm and an empty bed contact time (EBCT) of 10â15 minutes. That means for 1000 L/h, you need about 170â250 litres of GAC. Carbon block cartridges (5â10 micron) are simpler for small-scale: a 10-inch cartridge treats 5,000â10,000 litres before replacement. Always put a 5-micron sediment filter before the carbon to prevent clogging.

In Africa, coconut-shell carbon is preferred because it is hard, renewable, and has more micropores than coal-based carbon. It is produced in Ghana, Nigeria, and Tanzania. You can also make your own carbon from coconut shells or rice husks by burning them at 600â800Â°C with limited air, then activating with steam. But for consistent quality, buy food-grade certified carbon. Test performance by measuring chlorine residual (should be zero after carbon) and taste. If water tastes flat or has a slight sulphur smell, the carbon may be exhaustedâreplace it. Carbon does not remove bacteria; in fact, bacteria can grow on carbon if water sits stagnant. So always disinfect after carbon (ozone or UV). Backwash GAC filters every 2â3 days with clean water to remove trapped particles. Replace GAC every 6â12 months depending on usage. For a 500 L/h plant, budget $50â$100 per year for carbon replacement.

lessons.title: Mineral Adjustment and Blending for Consistent Taste
lessons.body:
After RO or distillation, water is too pureâit tastes flat and can be aggressive to pipes and bottles. You must add minerals to reach a target TDS of 50â150 mg/L and a pH of 7.0â7.5. The most common blend uses calcium chloride (CaCl2), magnesium sulphate (MgSO4), and sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3). A simple recipe for 1000 litres of RO water: dissolve 50 g calcium chloride, 30 g magnesium sulphate, and 20 g sodium bicarbonate in 10 litres of RO water, then dose this concentrate into the main tank while stirring. This gives roughly 50 mg/L calcium, 15 mg/L magnesium, and 30 mg/L bicarbonate. Adjust to tasteâsome markets prefer a sweeter profile (more magnesium) or a crisper profile (more calcium).

For consistent taste, you must measure TDS and pH every batch. Use a calibrated TDS meter and pH meter. If TDS is below 50 mg/L, add more mineral concentrate; if above 150 mg/L, dilute with more RO water. In Africa, many bottlers use commercial mineral blends (e.g., âWater Mineral Additiveâ from South Africa or Kenya) that come with dosing instructions. These cost about $10â$20 per kilogram and treat 10,000â20,000 litres. Always mix minerals in a clean, food-grade tank. Never add minerals directly to bottlesâmix in a batch tank with a mechanical stirrer for 10 minutes.

Blending is also used to mix high-TDS water with low-TDS water to achieve a target. For example, if you have 500 litres of RO water (TDS 10) and 500 litres of spring water (TDS 300), blending gives 1000 litres at TDS 155. This is common in Kenya and Uganda where spring water is abundant. But blending does not remove contaminantsâonly mix with water that already meets safety standards. After mineral adjustment, run the water through a 1-micron filter and then UV or ozone before bottling. Record every batch: date, TDS, pH, and mineral amounts. This traceability is required by many African food safety authorities (e.g., KEBS, NAFDAC, SABS).

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of sedimentation in primary treatment?
quiz.explanation: Sedimentation allows heavy particles to sink to the bottom by gravity.

quiz.q: Which chemical is commonly used as a coagulant in water treatment?
quiz.explanation: Alum (aluminium sulphate) is a cheap and widely used coagulant.

quiz.q: What is the recommended dose of alum for coagulation?
quiz.explanation: A typical dose is 10â30 mg per litre of water.

quiz.q: How often should you backwash a rapid sand filter?
quiz.explanation: Backwashing every 1â2 days removes trapped dirt and maintains flow.

quiz.q: What natural coagulant can be used if alum is unavailable?
quiz.explanation: Crushed moringa seeds contain proteins that act as a coagulant.

quiz.q: What does reverse osmosis (RO) remove from water?
quiz.explanation: RO membranes reject most dissolved salts, heavy metals, and microbes.

quiz.q: What is the typical operating pressure for a small RO system?
quiz.explanation: Small RO systems typically operate at 10â15 bar.

quiz.q: Why is antiscalant added before RO membranes?
quiz.explanation: Antiscalant prevents mineral scale from forming on the membrane.

quiz.q: How often should RO pre-filters be replaced?
quiz.explanation: Pre-filters typically need replacement every 1â3 months.

quiz.q: What is a key difference between nanofiltration and reverse osmosis?
options: C) NF does not remove bacteria
D) NF produces more reject water
quiz.explanation: Nanofiltration rejects 50â90% of salts, while RO rejects 95â99%.

quiz.q: What is the typical energy consumption for distilling 1 litre of water?
quiz.explanation: Boiling 1 litre of water takes about 0.7 kWh of electricity.

quiz.q: What is the TDS of distilled water?
quiz.explanation: Distillation leaves behind almost all dissolved solids, giving TDS < 5 mg/L.

quiz.q: What is the main danger of deionization (DI) resins?
options: B) They require dangerous chemicals for regeneration
quiz.explanation: Regeneration uses hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide, which are hazardous.

quiz.q: Why must distilled water be remineralised before bottling?
options: B) It tastes flat and is acidic
quiz.explanation: Distilled water lacks minerals, tastes flat, and has a low pH.

quiz.q: What is the recommended TDS range for bottled drinking water after mineral adjustment?
quiz.explanation: A TDS of 50â150 mg/L provides good taste and mineral balance.

quiz.q: How does ozone kill microbes?
options: B) By oxidising their cell walls
quiz.explanation: Ozone is a strong oxidant that destroys microbial cell walls.

quiz.q: What is the typical ozone dose for water disinfection?
quiz.explanation: A dose of 0.2â0.5 mg/L with contact time is effective.

quiz.q: What safety precaution is required when using ozone?
options: B) Install an ozone destruct unit
quiz.explanation: Ozone is toxic to breathe, so an ozone destruct unit is essential.

quiz.q: What UV dose is needed to inactivate bacteria and viruses?
quiz.explanation: A minimum UV dose of 40 mJ/cm2 is required for effective disinfection.

quiz.q: How often should UV lamps be replaced?
quiz.explanation: UV lamps lose intensity over time and should be replaced every 9,000 hours.

quiz.q: Why must water be pre-filtered before UV disinfection?
options: B) To prevent particles from shielding microbes
quiz.explanation: Particles can block UV light and protect microorganisms.

quiz.q: What does activated carbon remove from water?
quiz.explanation: Activated carbon adsorbs chlorine, pesticides, and taste/odour compounds.

quiz.q: What is the recommended empty bed contact time (EBCT) for GAC filters?
quiz.explanation: An EBCT of 10â15 minutes ensures adequate contact for adsorption.

quiz.q: Why is coconut-shell carbon preferred in Africa?
options: B) It is harder and has more micropores
quiz.explanation: Coconut-shell carbon is hard and has a high micropore volume for better adsorption.

quiz.q: What should you do if carbon-filtered water has a sulphur smell?
quiz.explanation: A sulphur smell indicates the carbon is exhausted and needs replacement.

quiz.q: Why must you disinfect after activated carbon filtration?
quiz.explanation: Bacteria can grow on carbon, so disinfection after carbon is necessary.

quiz.q: What is the target pH for bottled drinking water after mineral adjustment?
quiz.explanation: A pH of 7.0â7.5 is ideal for taste and stability.

quiz.q: Which minerals are commonly added to RO water for taste?
options: B) Calcium chloride, magnesium sulphate, sodium bicarbonate
quiz.explanation: These three minerals provide a balanced mineral profile.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of blending high-TDS water with low-TDS water?
options: B) To achieve a target TDS
quiz.explanation: Blending adjusts the final TDS to a desired level.

quiz.q: What record must be kept for each batch of bottled water?
options: A) Date, TDS, pH, mineral amounts
quiz.explanation: Traceability records are required by many African food safety authorities.
